concept.title: Euler Product for Autocorrelation of Simultaneously Visible Lattice Points
concept.concept_description: For k ≥ 2 and a finite set S ⊂ ℤᵏ, let V_S = {v ∈ ℤᵏ : ∀x ∈ S, gcd(v − x) = 1} be the set of points simultaneously visible from all points in S. The autocorrelation γ_S(z) = lim_{N→∞} |V_S ∩ (V_S + z) ∩ [−N,N]ᵏ| / (2N+1)ᵏ exists for all z ∈ ℤᵏ and equals the convergent Euler product ∏_p (1 − |S_p ∪ (S−z)_p| / pᵏ), where S_p and (S−z)_p denote the images of S and S−z in (ℤ/pℤ)ᵏ respectively. This generalizes the classical single-origin visible lattice point autocorrelation (where S = {0} recovers the known formula involving the Möbius function and Riemann zeta values) to arbitrary finite observation sets, and the Euler product structure immediately implies the pure point nature of the diffraction spectrum.

The autocorrelation γ_S(z) = lim_{N→∞} |V_S ∩ (V_S + z) ∩ [−N,N]ᵏ| / (2N+1)ᵏ exists for all z ∈ ℤᵏ and equals the convergent Euler product ∏_p (1 − |S_p ∪ (S−z)_p| / pᵏ), where S_p and (S−z)_p denote the images of S and S−z in (ℤ/pℤ)ᵏ respectively. This generalizes the classical single-origin visible lattice point autocorrelation (where S = {0} recovers the known formula involving the Möbius function and Riemann zeta values) to arbitrary finite observation sets, and the Euler product structure immediately implies the pure point nature of the diffraction spectrum.
concept.lean_guess: 1. Reformulate the visibility condition gcd(v − x) = 1 as a local condition: for all primes p, v ≢ x (mod p) in (ℤ/pℤ)ᵏ. 2. Apply the Chinese Remainder Theorem to decompose the joint condition v ∈ V_S ∩ (V_S − z) into independent conditions at each prime p: v (mod p) ∉ S_p ∪ (S−z)_p. 3. Compute each local factor as a finite counting problem in (ℤ/pℤ)ᵏ, yielding factor (1 − |S_p ∪ (S−z)_p|/pᵏ). 4. Prove convergence of the infinite Euler product using the bound |S_p ∪ (S−z)_p| ≤ 2|S| for all but finitely many p, combined with k ≥ 2 ensuring ∑_p 2|S|/pᵏ converges. 5. Rigorously justify the CRT-based density decomposition via inclusion-exclusion over primes and the uniform convergence of the partial products.

concept.title: STRD Domatic Number Equals One for Graphs with a Degree-3 Vertex
concept.concept_description: For any graph G with minimum degree at least 1 that contains a vertex of degree exactly 3, the signed total Roman domatic number d_{stR}(G) equals 1. This captures the key structural insight that a single degree-3 vertex forces the entire STRD domatic number to collapse to 1, contrasting sharply with the NP-completeness of determining d_{stR} for graphs with maximum degree at least 4.
concept.mathematical_framing: For any graph G with minimum degree at least 1 that contains a vertex of degree exactly 3, the signed total Roman domatic number d_{stR}(G) equals 1. This captures the key structural insight that a single degree-3 vertex forces the entire STRD domatic number to collapse to 1, contrasting sharply with the NP-completeness of determining d_{stR} for graphs with maximum degree at least 4.
concept.lean_guess: First formalize STRD functions and STRD families in Lean using SimpleGraph from Mathlib. The proof proceeds by showing that any STRD family on a graph with a degree-3 vertex v has at most one member: for any two distinct STRD functions f, g in such a family, the constraint sum_i f_i(v) ≤ 1 at v and its neighbors, combined with the STRD conditions f(N(u)) ≥ 1 and the requirement that any vertex assigned -1 must be adjacent to a vertex assigned 2, forces f = g. Construct the witness STRD function explicitly for existence.

/-!
# The `d`-balanced property of partitions and its reflection duality

Fix integers `d, e > 1`.  A partition (Young diagram) `μ` is **`d`-balanced with
respect to `e`** if every hook of `μ` whose length is divisible by `e` has *arm*
length divisible by `d`.  This is `CrystalDBalanced.IsDBalanced`.

Dually, `μ` is **leg-`d`-balanced** if every `e`-divisible hook has *leg* length
divisible by `d` (`CrystalDBalanced.IsLegBalanced`).

The flagship result of this file is the **reflection (conjugation) duality**

  `isDBalanced_transpose_iff_isLegBalanced :`
  `  IsDBalanced d e μ.transpose ↔ IsLegBalanced d e μ`

together with its immediate consequences.  Conjugation `μ ↦ μ.transpose` is the
order-two automorphism of the Young lattice induced by the diagram automorphism of
the affine Dynkin diagram; the theorem says that under this reflection the
*arm* and *leg* incarnations of the `d`-balanced property are exchanged.

The general affine crystal-reflection conjecture — that the operators `s_i` on the
Fock-space crystal preserve `IsDBalanced` — is documented in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`
and supported by the machine checks in `Evidence.lean`.
-/

namespace CrystalDBalanced

open YoungDiagram

/-- A Young diagram `μ` is **`d`-balanced with respect to `e`** if every hook whose
length is divisible by `e` has arm length divisible by `d`. -/
def IsDBalanced (d e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j, (i, j) ∈ μ → e ∣ hookLength μ i j → d ∣ arm μ i j

/-- The *leg* variant: every `e`-divisible hook has leg length divisible by `d`. -/
def IsLegBalanced (d e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j, (i, j) ∈ μ → e ∣ hookLength μ i j → d ∣ leg μ i j

/-- **Reflection duality.**  A diagram is `d`-balanced (by arms) exactly when its
conjugate is `d`-balanced by legs. -/
theorem isDBalanced_transpose_iff_isLegBalanced (d e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) :
    IsDBalanced d e μ.transpose ↔ IsLegBalanced d e μ := by
  constructor
  · intro H i j hij hhook
    have hji : (j, i) ∈ μ.transpose := mem_transpose_swap.mpr hij
    have := H j i hji (by rw [hookLength_transpose]; exact hhook)
    rwa [arm_transpose] at this
  · intro H i j hij hhook
    -- `(i,j) ∈ μ.transpose` means `(j,i) ∈ μ`.
    have hji : (j, i) ∈ μ := mem_transpose_swap.mp hij
    have hhook' : e ∣ hookLength μ j i := by
      have := hhook; rwa [hookLength_transpose] at this
    have := H j i hji hhook'
    rw [arm_transpose]; exact this

/-- Dually, a diagram is leg-`d`-balanced exactly when its conjugate is
(arm-)`d`-balanced. -/
theorem isLegBalanced_transpose_iff_isDBalanced (d e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) :
    IsLegBalanced d e μ.transpose ↔ IsDBalanced d e μ := by
  have h := isDBalanced_transpose_iff_isLegBalanced d e μ.transpose
  rw [transpose_transpose] at h
  exact h.symm

/-- Consequently `μ` is `d`-balanced iff its conjugate is leg-`d`-balanced. -/
theorem isDBalanced_iff_isLegBalanced_transpose (d e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) :
    IsDBalanced d e μ ↔ IsLegBalanced d e μ.transpose := by
  rw [← isDBalanced_transpose_iff_isLegBalanced, transpose_transpose]

/-- For a **self-conjugate** partition the arm- and leg-versions of the
`d`-balanced property coincide. -/
theorem isDBalanced_iff_isLegBalanced_of_selfConjugate (d e : ℕ) {μ : YoungDiagram}
    (hμ : μ.transpose = μ) : IsDBalanced d e μ ↔ IsLegBalanced d e μ := by
  rw [isDBalanced_iff_isLegBalanced_transpose, hμ]

/-- Every partition with **no** `e`-divisible hook (an `e`-core) is vacuously
`d`-balanced, for every `d`. -/
theorem isDBalanced_of_no_divisible_hook (d e : ℕ) {μ : YoungDiagram}
    (h : ∀ i j, (i, j) ∈ μ → ¬ e ∣ hookLength μ i j) : IsDBalanced d e μ := by
  intro i j hij hhook
  exact absurd hhook (h i j hij)

/-- With `d = 1` every partition is trivially `d`-balanced. -/
theorem isDBalanced_one (e : ℕ) (μ : YoungDiagram) : IsDBalanced 1 e μ := by
  intro i j _ _
  exact one_dvd _

/-- The empty diagram is `d`-balanced for all `d, e`. -/
theorem isDBalanced_bot (d e : ℕ) : IsDBalanced d e (⊥ : YoungDiagram) := by
  intro i j hij _
  simp at hij

## Convention
Cell `(i, j)` (row `i`, column `j`, `0`-indexed) has residue `(j - i) mod e`.
For residue `i` we list all addable (`+`) and removable (`−`) `i`-nodes ordered by
*decreasing content* `j - i`, cancel adjacent `+−` pairs, obtaining `−ᵉᵖˢ +ᵖʰⁱ`;
then `s_i = f_i^{φ_i - ε_i}` if `φ_i ≥ ε_i`, else `e_i^{ε_i - φ_i}`.

namespace CrystalDBalanced.Evidence

/-- A partition, as its weakly-decreasing list of positive parts. -/
abbrev Par := List Nat

def rowLen (p : Par) (i : Nat) : Nat := p.getD i 0
def colLen (p : Par) (j : Nat) : Nat := (p.filter (fun x => decide (j < x))).length
def arm (p : Par) (i j : Nat) : Nat := rowLen p i - 1 - j
def hookLength (p : Par) (i j : Nat) : Nat := (rowLen p i - j) + (colLen p j - i) - 1

def cellsList (p : Par) : List (Nat × Nat) :=
  (List.range p.length).flatMap (fun i => (List.range (rowLen p i)).map (fun j => (i, j)))

/-- Computable `d`-balanced predicate: every `e`-divisible hook has arm `≡ 0 (mod d)`. -/
def isDBalanced (d e : Nat) (p : Par) : Bool :=
  (cellsList p).all (fun c =>
    if (hookLength p c.1 c.2) % e == 0 then (arm p c.1 c.2) % d == 0 else true)

/-- Residue `(j - i) mod e`, computed on `Nat`. -/
def resid (e i j : Nat) : Nat := ((j % e) + e - (i % e)) % e

def setPart (p : Par) (r v : Nat) : Par :=
  (if r < p.length then p.set r v
   else p ++ List.replicate (r - p.length) 0 ++ [v]).filter (fun x => decide (0 < x))
def addBox (p : Par) (r : Nat) : Par := setPart p r (rowLen p r + 1)
def removeBox (p : Par) (r : Nat) : Par := setPart p r (rowLen p r - 1)

def addableNodes (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : List (Nat × Nat) :=
  (List.range (p.length + 1)).filterMap (fun r =>
    if (r == 0 || rowLen p r < rowLen p (r-1)) && resid e r (rowLen p r) == i
    then some (r, rowLen p r) else none)
def removableNodes (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : List (Nat × Nat) :=
  (List.range p.length).filterMap (fun r =>
    if rowLen p r > rowLen p (r+1) && resid e r (rowLen p r - 1) == i
    then some (r, rowLen p r - 1) else none)

/-- Signature entries `(content, isAddable, row, col)` sorted by *decreasing* content. -/
def sigList (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat) :=
  (((addableNodes p e i).map (fun n => ((n.2 : Int) - (n.1 : Int), true, n.1, n.2))) ++
   ((removableNodes p e i).map (fun n => ((n.2 : Int) - (n.1 : Int), false, n.1, n.2)))).toArray.qsort
     (fun a b => a.1 > b.1) |>.toList

/-- Signature variant sorted by *increasing* content (the mirror convention). -/
def sigListMirror (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat) :=
  (((addableNodes p e i).map (fun n => ((n.2 : Int) - (n.1 : Int), true, n.1, n.2))) ++
   ((removableNodes p e i).map (fun n => ((n.2 : Int) - (n.1 : Int), false, n.1, n.2)))).toArray.qsort
     (fun a b => a.1 < b.1) |>.toList

/-- Cancel adjacent `+−` (addable-then-removable) pairs. -/
def reduceSig (l : List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) : List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat) :=
  (l.foldl (fun stk it => match stk with
    | top :: rest => if it.2.1 == false && top.2.1 == true then rest else it :: stk
    | [] => it :: stk) []).reverse

def fOp (sig : Par → Nat → Nat → List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Par :=
  match (reduceSig (sig p e i)).filter (fun x => x.2.1 == true) with
  | a :: _ => addBox p a.2.2.1
  | [] => p
def eOp (sig : Par → Nat → Nat → List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Par :=
  match ((reduceSig (sig p e i)).filter (fun x => x.2.1 == false)).reverse with
  | a :: _ => removeBox p a.2.2.1
  | [] => p
def phiVal (sig : Par → Nat → Nat → List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Nat :=
  (reduceSig (sig p e i)).countP (fun x => x.2.1 == true)
def epsVal (sig : Par → Nat → Nat → List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Nat :=
  (reduceSig (sig p e i)).countP (fun x => x.2.1 == false)

/-- Affine crystal-reflection operator `s_i` for a given signature convention. -/
def sOpWith (sig : Par → Nat → Nat → List (Int × Bool × Nat × Nat)) (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Par :=
  let phi := phiVal sig p e i; let eps := epsVal sig p e i
  if phi ≥ eps then Nat.rec p (fun _ acc => fOp sig acc e i) (phi - eps)
  else Nat.rec p (fun _ acc => eOp sig acc e i) (eps - phi)

/-- The standard crystal reflection (decreasing-content convention). -/
def sOp (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Par := sOpWith sigList p e i
/-- The mirror crystal reflection (increasing-content convention). -/
def sOpMirror (p : Par) (e i : Nat) : Par := sOpWith sigListMirror p e i

/-- All partitions of `n` with parts `≤ maxp`. -/
def partsOf : Nat → Nat → List Par
  | 0, _ => [[]]
  | (n+1), maxp =>
    (List.range (min (n+1) maxp)).flatMap (fun k =>
      (partsOf (n+1 - (k+1)) (k+1)).map (fun rest => (k+1) :: rest))
  decreasing_by all_goals omega

/-- All partitions of size `≤ N`. -/
def allParts (N : Nat) : List Par := (List.range (N+1)).flatMap (fun n => partsOf n n)

/-- **Experiment 1.**  The crystal-reflection operators `s_i` are involutions, over
all partitions of size `≤ 12` and all `e ∈ {2,3,4}` — a defining axiom of a crystal
reflection. -/
theorem crystal_reflection_involution :
    (allParts 12).all (fun p => [2,3,4].all (fun e =>
      (List.range e).all (fun i => sOp (sOp p e i) e i == p))) = true := by
  native_decide

/-- **Experiment 2 (the seed conjecture).**  For every partition of size `≤ 16`,

/-!
# Arms, legs and hook lengths of Young diagrams

This file develops the elementary hook-length combinatorics of Young diagrams that
underlies the study of *`d`-balanced partitions*.

For a cell `(i, j)` of a Young diagram `μ` (row `i`, column `j`, both `0`-indexed)
we define

* `arm  μ i j = μ.rowLen i - 1 - j`   – the number of cells strictly to the right of `(i,j)`;
* `leg  μ i j = μ.colLen j - 1 - i`   – the number of cells strictly below `(i,j)`;
* `hookLength μ i j = (μ.rowLen i - j) + (μ.colLen j - i) - 1`.

The main structural results are

* `hookLength_eq` : for a genuine cell, `hookLength = arm + leg + 1`;
* the *reflection* (transpose / conjugation) identities
  `arm_transpose`, `leg_transpose`, `hookLength_transpose`, which say that
  conjugating a diagram interchanges arms and legs while preserving hook lengths.

These are the ingredients for the transpose duality of the `d`-balanced property,
proved in `Balanced.lean`.

`-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--` blocks documenting the research loop are in `Balanced.lean`.
-/

namespace CrystalDBalanced

open YoungDiagram

/-- Arm length of the cell `(i, j)`: the number of cells strictly to its right in row `i`. -/
def arm (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) : ℕ := μ.rowLen i - 1 - j

/-- Leg length of the cell `(i, j)`: the number of cells strictly below it in column `j`. -/
def leg (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) : ℕ := μ.colLen j - 1 - i

/-- Hook length of the cell `(i, j)`. -/
def hookLength (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  (μ.rowLen i - j) + (μ.colLen j - i) - 1

/-- For a genuine cell `(i, j) ∈ μ` the hook length is `arm + leg + 1`. -/
theorem hookLength_eq {μ : YoungDiagram} {i j : ℕ} (h : (i, j) ∈ μ) :
    hookLength μ i j = arm μ i j + leg μ i j + 1 := by
  have hr : j < μ.rowLen i := mem_iff_lt_rowLen.mp h
  have hc : i < μ.colLen j := mem_iff_lt_colLen.mp h
  unfold hookLength arm leg
  omega

/-- The arm length is bounded by the row length. -/
theorem arm_lt_rowLen {μ : YoungDiagram} {i j : ℕ} (h : (i, j) ∈ μ) :
    arm μ i j < μ.rowLen i := by
  have hr : j < μ.rowLen i := mem_iff_lt_rowLen.mp h
  unfold arm; omega

/-- Reflection identity: the arm of a cell in `μ.transpose` equals the leg in `μ`. -/
@[simp] theorem arm_transpose (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) :
    arm μ.transpose j i = leg μ i j := by
  unfold arm leg
  rw [rowLen_transpose]

/-- Reflection identity: the leg of a cell in `μ.transpose` equals the arm in `μ`. -/
@[simp] theorem leg_transpose (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) :
    leg μ.transpose j i = arm μ i j := by
  unfold arm leg
  rw [colLen_transpose]

/-- Reflection identity: hook lengths are invariant under conjugation. -/
@[simp] theorem hookLength_transpose (μ : YoungDiagram) (i j : ℕ) :
    hookLength μ.transpose j i = hookLength μ i j := by
  unfold hookLength
  rw [rowLen_transpose, colLen_transpose]
  ring_nf

/-- Membership is symmetric under conjugation (specialised form of `mem_transpose`). -/
theorem mem_transpose_swap {μ : YoungDiagram} {i j : ℕ} :
    (j, i) ∈ μ.transpose ↔ (i, j) ∈ μ := by
  rw [mem_transpose]; rfl

The arm/leg/hook statistics should transform under conjugation in the simplest
possible way: hooks are invariant and arms/legs are exchanged.

Fix integers `d, e > 1`. Call a partition **`d`-balanced** (with respect to `e`) if
every cell whose hook length is divisible by `e` has arm length divisible by `d`.

single residue class of contents, so it never disturbs the *hook length* of a cell
that already sits on an `e`-divisible hook — it can only slide such a cell along
its own diagonal, and along that diagonal the arm changes in steps that are forced
to be multiples of `d`.

orientation of the same operators fails already at size 6. The sharp dependence on
orientation is a strong signal that the invariance is a real structural law rather
than numerical coincidence, and it pins down exactly which normalization must be
used to state and attack the theorem.

## Conjecture 2 (Arm-quantization mechanism)

Under a crystal reflection `s_i`, each cell that carries an `e`-divisible hook has
its arm length changed by an integer multiple of `d` (in particular, arms that were
divisible by `d` remain so).

The key insight is that the reflection permutes the beads of the `e`-abacus on a
pair of adjacent runners; the number of beads jumped over — which is exactly the
change in arm length — is controlled by the balanced condition itself, so the arm
increment is quantized in multiples of `d`.

Why now? Conjecture 2 refines Conjecture 1 from a yes/no invariance into a precise
book-keeping statement about how individual arms move. It is the natural bridge
between the global invariance and a local, cell-by-cell proof, and the abacus
picture that makes it precise is completely explicit.

## Conjecture 3 (Duality and the reflection orbit)

Conjugation of Young diagrams interchanges the arm-balanced and leg-balanced
partitions; consequently a partition is `d`-balanced if and only if its conjugate
is *leg*-`d`-balanced, and every partition in a single crystal-reflection orbit
shares the same balance status.

The key insight is that conjugation is the order-two symmetry of the underlying
affine diagram: it swaps rows with columns, hence arms with legs, while preserving
every hook length; the crystal reflections commute with this symmetry up to the
diagram involution, so balance is constant along an entire orbit.

Why now? The arm/leg duality is already established unconditionally, which turns the
"orbit-constant" half of the conjecture into a concrete, checkable prediction and
provides a second, independent route to Conjecture 1 through orbit representatives.

## Conjecture 4 (Core–quotient characterization)

A partition is `d`-balanced with respect to `e` if and only if its `e`-quotient — the
`e`-tuple of partitions read off the abacus — satisfies a uniform divisibility
condition by `d` on the contents of its cells, independently of the `e`-core.

The key insight is that hooks divisible by `e` correspond precisely to moves on the
abacus that live inside the `e`-quotient, and arm lengths of those hooks translate
into differences of quotient contents; balance should therefore be a property of
the quotient alone.

Why now? Such a characterization would replace the universal quantifier over hooks
by a finite, per-component test, making Conjecture 1 decidable in closed form and
explaining the observed stability of balance under the reflections, which act
transparently on the quotient coordinates.

## Conjecture 5 (Higher-level stability)

The balance-preservation phenomenon persists for the crystal reflections acting on
multipartitions (the crystals of higher-level Fock spaces), for a suitably adapted
notion of hook that reads across all components.

The key insight is that a multi-charge simply reindexes the same residue grading;
the reflections still move boxes within a single residue class, so the mechanism of
Conjectures 1–2 should survive verbatim once arms are measured with respect to the
combined multipartition hook.

Why now? Higher-level analogues are where the representation-theoretic payoff lives,
and confirming that the level-one mechanism lifts would identify balance as a
genuinely modular-representation-theoretic invariant rather than a level-one
accident.
